explication:
1. This is a multi-product monorepo centered on a Rust terminal coding agent, plus a separate web presence and some deployment/integration glue. The main user-facing runtime is split into two Rust binaries: `deepseek` as the dispatcher CLI (`crates/cli`) and `deepseek-tui` as the interactive terminal app (`crates/tui`). The README’s install flow makes clear both binaries are part of the core product.

2. The primary runtime path is: user command → CLI dispatcher → TUI runtime → async agent engine → OpenAI-compatible streaming model API. The engine owns turn execution, streaming reasoning blocks, tool invocation, and session progression. The TUI is not just a view; it is the interactive front end that feeds user input and renders streamed agent output.

3. The Rust workspace is layered into reusable libraries under `crates/` and product binaries on top. Shared subsystems include `config`, `core`, `protocol`, `state`, `tools`, `hooks`, `mcp`, `secrets`, `execpolicy`, `tui-core`, and `agent`. This structure suggests a clean boundary between stable libraries and the interactive application shell.

4. The core agent engine lives in `crates/tui/src/core/engine/*` and is the orchestration boundary for a turn. From the file layout, it is responsible for dispatch, approvals, streaming, tool setup, tool execution, context handling, and loop control. That engine sits between model responses and side effects on the local machine.

5. Tooling is a major architectural subsystem, not a thin helper layer. The tool catalog spans shell, file, git, search, web fetch/search, patch application, diagnostics, tasking, review, memory, skills, subagents, and more. Tools appear to be mediated through a typed registry and routed back into the transcript, which means tool results are first-class agent inputs rather than ad hoc command outputs.

6. There is a deliberate safety boundary around local effects. The README calls out approval gates, Plan/Agent/YOLO modes, and OS-level sandboxing via Seatbelt on macOS, Landlock on Linux, and Job Objects on Windows. The `execpolicy`, `network_policy`, `workspace_trust`, and `command_safety` modules indicate that file, shell, and network actions are filtered before execution.

7. Session and workspace state are persisted separately from the live UI. The repository includes session managers, snapshot/restore logic, stash/recovery, and side-git rollback behavior that does not touch the repo’s own `.git`. This means the architecture intentionally treats agent activity as replayable and recoverable state, not just an ephemeral terminal conversation.

8. The model interaction layer is provider-aware and streaming-oriented. The README documents DeepSeek, OpenAI-compatible endpoints, NVIDIA NIM, OpenRouter, Novita, Fireworks, SGLang, vLLM, and Ollama. Auto mode routes each turn through a small model-selection call before sending the real request, so provider/model selection is part of runtime orchestration rather than a static config choice.

9. Several “capability expansion” subsystems plug into the main agent loop: MCP servers, sub-agents, and native RLM sessions. MCP extends available tooling across external servers; sub-agents run concurrently with their own context and tool registry; RLM provides persistent REPL-style child sessions for batched analysis. These are all boundary-crossing features, but they remain mediated by the same session/turn machinery.

10. The terminal UI is a large subsystem in its own right, with composer, command palette, session picker, model/provider pickers, markdown rendering, streaming transcript views, notifications, onboarding, and keybinding management. The `tui` crate appears to own both presentation and interaction logic, while `tui-core` holds lower-level rendering or interaction primitives reused by the app.

11. Diagnostics and local developer feedback are integrated into the agent loop. The repo includes LSP client/registry modules and reads like it surfaces post-edit diagnostics back into the session before the next model turn. That makes the system a closed loop: edit → lint/diagnose → feed back into context → continue reasoning.

12. Skills are a separate content/plugin layer. Skills are discovered from workspace and global directories, bundled into the app, and exposed through slash commands like `/skills` and `/skill`. Architecturally, skills are instruction assets that influence model behavior, not executable plugins in the traditional sense.

13. Distribution is handled as a product ecosystem around the Rust core. There is an npm wrapper package under `npm/deepseek-tui`, Docker packaging, Homebrew/CNB scripts, and release automation in GitHub Actions. The npm package is explicitly an installer/wrapper for release binaries, not the runtime itself, so the real application boundary stays in Rust.

14. The repository also contains a separate Next.js web app under `web/`, which is not part of the terminal agent runtime. That web system has public pages, admin routes, GitHub/feed integrations, Cloudflare Worker/KV plumbing, and localization. It functions more like the project’s marketing/community/control plane than the core agent engine.

15. There is also an integration service for Feishu/Lark under `integrations/feishu-bridge`, plus Tencent/CNB/Lighthouse deployment scripts and docs. That indicates a remote-first operational path where the terminal agent can be paired with messaging and cloud-hosted workspace infrastructure, but these are adjunct systems around the main local runtime.
